question: Prove that the square of a skew-symmetric matrix is symmetric, and hence verify the result for $$K=\begin{bmatrix}0&1&-2\\-1&0&3\\2&-3&0\end{bmatrix}$$ by explicitly calculating $K^2$.
explanation:
Proof of the Required Result

Let $A$ be a skew-symmetric matrix. Then, by definition, $$A'=-A$$ Consider the transpose of $A^2$. Using the property $(AB)'=B'A'$, $$(A^2)'=(AA)'=A'A'$$ Since $A'=-A$, $$(A^2)'=(-A)(-A)=A^2$$ Therefore, $(A^2)'=A^2$, which proves that $A^2$ is symmetric.

Verification for the Given Matrix

For $$K=\begin{bmatrix}0&1&-2\\-1&0&3\\2&-3&0\end{bmatrix},$$ we have $K'=-K$, so $K$ is skew-symmetric. Now, $$K^2=\begin{bmatrix}0&1&-2\\-1&0&3\\2&-3&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0&1&-2\\-1&0&3\\2&-3&0\end{bmatrix}$$ $$=\begin{bmatrix}-5&6&3\\6&-10&2\\3&2&-13\end{bmatrix}$$ Taking its transpose, $$(K^2)'=\begin{bmatrix}-5&6&3\\6&-10&2\\3&2&-13\end{bmatrix}=K^2$$ Hence, $K^2$ is symmetric, verifying the proved result for the given skew-symmetric matrix.
